text: Upgraded from 1070 to 4070 Ti (a 2-slot model from INNO3D which is the best I can fit in my build). Undervolted it a bit to 925 mV/2640 MHz. And there IS generation change since 3000 series but it's not so much in absolute performance but rather in power efficiency at lower voltage. It becomes obvious once you undervolt. Can I get the same perf in Cyberpunk 2077 from 3090 Ti at 150 Watt? Of course not, not even close. The only downside is the price but it's the same problem with pretty much every decent GPU nowadays.

text:
I guess releasing a card that matches a titan class GPU from last generation while consuming half the power for half the price is too much because of the label slapped on it. I own a 4070Ti, upgraded from a 6700XT and the performance differences are night and day, add frame generation and chances are I'm not going to be upgrading every two years like I did with AMD. 

Did Nvidia fudge the naming scheme? Yes. Did they fudge the performance? Nope. 

Yes, the card is expensive as shit, but you get a phenomenal card and that's even before adding DLSS 3.0 and FG. I haven't found many reviews that touch up on Frame Generation considering it's in quite a few titles, but damn Nvidia literally just said here, since we're charging you your first born and a liver and kidney, here's a free feature that'll boost your frame rate by 25-40% that requires minimal hardware overhead, and yes we know it can add latency so here's another feature to combat that. 

Nvidia's new cards value should be weighted at the value that DLSS 3.0 and Frame Generation + Reflex bring to the table, not just the generational performance gains. If coded right Frame Generation can be turned on separate from DLSS, so the performance bump from let's say your 3080-3080Ti might be 15-20%, but turn on FG and that all of a sudden turns into a 35-40% jump with minimal impact to image quality. 

I went from a 6700XT to a 4070Ti, I was seriously eyeballing and praying AMD would knock it out of the park with the 7000 series, and they did with rasterization performance, but when I saw the reviews on Frame Generation and the videos showing the difference it made me turn my focus to Nvidia, and boy am I glad I didn't buy the 7900XT. Yes, it has more VRAM and a bigger bus, but the value between the two heavily favors the 4070Ti, to a point to where it's like why does the 7900XT even exist? 

Then I looked at the lower end offerings AMD was launching later this year and saw that they were maybe 25-30% bumps in performance, with RT performance that's behind Nvidia, and no other features to speak of until FSR 3.0 came out, and even then it's adoption rate might just fall victim to the same adoption rate of FSR 2.0--and honestly, I have to say this: I'm happy with my purchase, regardless of cost, it's exceeded even my wildest expectations for the resolution I game at (2560x1440), and runs cool and shit that power draw is something else. On average it pulls as much wattage as my fully maxed out 6700XT while giving me a tremendous leap in performance.

text:
Love seeing these 1440 frame rates of over 100 with 1%'s of 60+ being called "moderate gaming performance" How far we've moved on.
I struggle to see frame rates or feel refresh rates in control updates at around 90 - maybe 100 in very fast moving games where micro control is a must. But I'm not sure.
I've played games on a MSI G27 where the frame rate delivered to screen never drops below 165 and the control refresh is also always above 165. 
I cannot tell the difference - at all, even after extended play between that - and 90hz on my other monitor (with about 90 control input /refreshes per second)
I know many people can - esp. younger gamers (I'm 55) but I can't - not even a little bit - not even side by side testing. 
So the value prop of anything over 90 hz and an input response of less than 90th  of a second is zero for me, as I can't see or sense it.
I also benefit from having no use for 4K as unless the screen is about 40 inches and I'm 3 feet away from it, I can't see the pixel detail or see any difference in image quality between that and 1440 on a (large but more manageable) 37" screen.
So I'll never need a high end graphics card, and I'll never need a 4K monitor. I would be wasting money as I can't sense the benefits they bring to the table - even a little bit.  :)

text: People need to realize that this is a bad purchase. The average consumer won't care, but the techie people will. For starters, one of the major issues with the 4070 Ti is the gimped 192-Bit memory bus. The 3070 came with a 256-Bit bus, and that extra bandwidth matters! Also, a 3070 costs only $500-$600 now. A 192- Bit bus that 3060 uses, and you're paying $800+ for that! Ok, so why the 192-Bit Bus then? Easy... Profit! Why? Hear me out. The performance you're seeing from the 4070 Ti is with DLSS 3.0 enabled... A software trick to give you more frames. The thing is, I'd rather have the pure raw bandwidth of a 256 Bit-Bus that can be used on ALL GAMES. DLSS is pretty game specific. Having a trimmed down bus means you're going to have performance problems with other games, or be no better than the 30 series offerings!! I'm hanging onto my 3070 and it's raw 256-Bit bus. Why would I pay $800.00 just to get 4 extra gigs of ram, that is essentially wasted unless you're trying to game at 4K, A little better ray tracing, (I don't really care about Ray Tracing, nor do any of my games support it) some AV1 encoder, and a DLSS 3.0 game specific "Cheat to simulate more frames through hackery"?? No, folks, you're paying too much for a card that should be $450.00. I am forced to wait for the 5000 series, or see what AMD/Intel has up their sleeve. Look past the DLSS BS and see what you're actually getting! You're getting ripped off!

text: I feel this generation of CPUs and GPUs are largely a big disappointment. When Nvidia first launched the RTX 4090, it kind of get people all excited looking at the performance. But the moment we go down 1 level, the performance plunged at least 20%. Move down another level, we lose another north of 20% performance. To be honest, I am not at all shocked by the poor performance. What Nvidia is doing this generation, it is not different from what AMD did with the RDNA2, and that is they cut the specs too hard. Just like Navi 21 to 23, the card lost 50% or CUs, cache and fortunately, not that much memory bus. In the case of the RTX 4070 Ti, I feel the 50% cut in memory bus probably killed performance, since we can clearly see that the card suffers at higher resolution and with RT enabled. It is not a bad card, but is ruined by its price. If anyone already own or can buy a RTX 3080 cheap, might as well stick to it.

text:
​ @nattybuffalodread  IIRC there's a word for it already. "Oligopoly", which is when a small number of firms create a product desired by a large number of consumers. Notable, you don't actually need AND deliberate price fixing or back room deals in an oligopoly. I'm not say that NVIDIA and AMD aren't doing shady backroom deals, but in such a market, it's very easy to coordinate an effective monopoly just by looking at what your handful of competitors are doing right out in the open.
 
The more competitors you have though, the harder this becomes without resorting to illegal price fixing that would trip regulations and business laws. And also the more likely that one of your competitors will 'defect' to grow their market share at your expense. 
 
Interestingly enough there's also an inverse in economics. An 'Oligopsony' which is when a small number of powerful buyers exist for a product or service. Which in theory is the point of allowing both strong (well regulated) private insurance and at least last resort government option for health insurance as both of those should be putting pressure on medical companies as their main source of business.

text:
The entire point of this card is DLSS 3.0. If you're not going to use it, don't buy a 4000 series card. Of course it's not apples to apples because Nvidia has a new technology that is only available on the 4000 series. So it should be comparing DLSS 2.0 on 3080 vs DLSS 3.0 on 4070ti, and there you will have performance improvements.

As for the 3x performance, I think it could be reasonable with only a slight decrease in graphics quality, as I would assume that DLSS 3.0 is better at creating more quality results when upscaling compared to DLSS 2.0 (at least in terms of fps). So a comparison between an RTX 3080 running on DLSS 2.0 quality (or no DLSS) and 4070ti running DLSS 3.0 quality with frame interpolation could potentially result in this level of performance difference for very GPU heavy games.

text:
So either specs are being overinflated with a 4080 12gb, or we are being price gouged with a 4070ti?   With that said the 4070ti still seems pretty comparable to a 3090 and not very far behind a 3090ti in just raster, which is pretty impressive, and much more comparable in price. Let's see 3090ti msrp $1099 vs similar raster performance 4070ti $799 plus frame generation.  Now turn on DLSS 3/frame generation and you can see the performance leap, although how much this is "cheating" I don't know as I haven't seen DLSS 3 with my own eyes. 

My question to Gamers Nexus, and it would be a great video, is if they think DLSS 3 (or more specifically frame generation) is never going to filter down to the 20x/30x cards because 1) those generations aren't fast enough or 2) because Nvidia wants to artificially make the 40x series more palatable?  I'll bet that it's because of reason 2, as someone already hacked this into their 20x card albeit with some instability.  Now if frame generation can truly be applied (or hacked) to at least 30x cards then Nvidia's lies would really crumble all around them.

text: For raster graphics hardware used to literally chase the beam. 60 FPS felt perfectly responsive. Early 3D games used straight double or triple buffering and this added a bit of latency; you needed somewhere around 100 FPS for it to feel as responsive as raster hardware at 60. Programning for multicore meant pipelining across multiple frames. 165 Hz monitors don’t even feel as responsive as 60 Hz used to; you have to really crank the framerate well above the refresh rate. Adding frame interpolation onto this means even more latency.

text:
I believe the high prices of these latest GPUs (and AMD also isn't really really cheap at 1000 bucks a piece) are a symptom of a larger issue. If you look at all those gaming benchmarks, the new cards (and oftentimes even the older gen) is able to run these games at 100+ FPS at 4K resolution. While if you look at Steam charts, a majority of players (64%) are still on 1080p. The 4K is using only 3% of players. Simply speaking, the GPUs are getting so powerful and so much ahead of what the games actually need, that only very little players feels the incentive to upgrade. And if that's the case then the companies might just as well put a premium price on these because they know only core fans or rich dudes would buy them and they don't really care about the price that much.

And the funny part is that it will only get worse. Just imagine. In 2 years we will get a new generation that will again offer another 60 or 80% more performance, but I doubt the games will be 60 to 80% more hardware intensive. Either the prices will get even higher for the next gen or we will see the performance gain much lower next time.

text:
Clearly there was a group inside of Nvidia that was completely and utterly convinced that DLSS 3 would let them sell these cards at extremely high prices. How this group won in the internal discussions is the real mystery, but there really is no other explanation. The greed on display defies logic unless you hyperfocus on that datapoint. This is so much worse than the 20 series launch. Honestly the most frustrating part about that launch was the long wait from pascal to turing. Getting cards with the same value proposition minus RT was such a sandbag after waiting over 2 years, but at least the value proposition didn't outright decrease.

At least the 20 series was an interesting paradigm shift for rendering akin to shader support in the past. It is and was a big deal to get hardware out there that supported those features, the biggest issue with turing wasn't the hardware so much as long dev cycles for games. The hardware had to exist with little bespoke support for the features at some point, that much is a fact.

DLSS 3 is cool, but I really don't think most people prefer ultra high framerates for the visual smoothness as much as the significantly improved responsiveness, which DLSS 3 makes worse (and no, comparing reflex enabled dlss 3 with no reflex enabled dlss 2 doesn't count). That said it's not just a gimmick, but it's not anywhere close to a cool enough hardware feature to justify what Nvidia has done with pricing.

author: @brohemian

text:
Mmm! Science and savagery! Exactly what I come to GN for :D

With this news, I think my "favorites" so far are the 4080 and the 7900XT. The 4080 honestly seems like a great card: it's just atrociously, offensively expensive. The performance is really good though, and it runs cool and doesn't suck an unreasonable amount of power. If price were not a factor and I could pick any card out of the current gen lineup to put in my PC, I'd install a 4080 since it strikes the best balance between performance and power draw (and so far it doesn't seem to have any manufacturing defects). In terms of "value" the 7900XT seems like the best card (available at it's $900 MSRP, has good raster performance, has reasonable power draw) but the coil whine problems make it a non-starter for me (I've had cards that squealed like that in the past and it was just insufferably irritating to me) and while I'd personally slap a waterblock on it, the defective OEM coolers probably make it a hard sell to most people. It also just generally feels bad to spend almost a thousand dollars on some third-tier also-ran product: for a grand you'd like to feel you were buying something upscale.

There's no way in fuck you'd ever convince me to buy a 4070 Ti for over ~$500. You know it's gonna end up actually costing ~$1000 street-price and the performance doesn't even justify the $800 FE MSRP in my opinion. Who wants to spend $800-1000 on a GPU that can't run Fortnite at 1440p high-refresh without turning down graphics settings? I think I'm just gonna skip this generation entirely. GTX 1080 still slaps: thanks EVGA for building a solid product and EK for selling spare parts for their waterblocks so I can keep it running.

text:
This is the same situation as the 1080 TI vs the 2080.  Basically no performance uplift with normal rasterization, but some actual increase with games that supported DLSS.  Plus, the 1080 Ti couldn't do RTX.  Well, not in such a way that you would ever want to play with it on anyway.  The biggest benefit to the 2080 was DLSS, and I suspect Nvidia thought they could do the same here with DLSS 3.0.  But that tech is pretty much NYI in just about every game out there.  Even DLSS 2.0 isn't ubiquitous enough yet to warrant the upgrade, which so far seems to amount to nothing more than "fake frames".  Yay, I can get my GPU to do motion interpolation like my TV, with less latency but more glitches!

This isn't the first time they've rebranded a card though. It's just the most expensive example.  Anyway, glad I decided to ignore this entire launch after they first revealed the prices of the 4090 and 4080.  Already have an EVGA 3080 FTW3U (😥) and I'll be fine until the 50 series...that will hopefully launch at $300 less at least for the 90 and 80.  I'll do a full system build then too.

text:
Nvidia rebadging the 4080 as a 4070Ti is still screwing over consumers. The whole point of the Ti is that it (almost always) uses the GPU die of the card above it, etc. GTX 980Ti used GM200 (Titan X) instead of the GM204 (GTX 980) die, GTX 1080Ti used GP102 (Titan Xp/X Pascal) instead of GP104 (GTX 1080). This should've been the 4070, if anything. It's incredibly pathetic as well to release the Ti version of a card before the actual card. Imagine how the RTX 4070 is going to look in comparison, once it comes out (assuming it does because nvidia are advertising the 30 series now for mainstream consumers 😂).

EDIT: I don't know why you keep pointing out the GT 1030 DDR4 as your main comparison for Nvidia releasing a severely nerfed product with the same name as a better one, when a much better comparison can be made with the GTX 1060 6GB and 3GB, which is almost the exact same situation as the RTX 4080 16GB and 12GB, aside from the use of different silicon (The 1060-3GB uses a cut down GP106 with 1152 shader cores instead of 1280, really it should've been called the 1050 Ti instead of what was).

author: @abdelrahmanaboelnasr

text: @abdelrahmanaboelnasr  But you're comparing a product that has a MUCH larger competition base to a product that really has only 1 competitor (discounting Intel as a GPU competitor). So in the hard drive business, you have to be a lot more competitive just to compete with all the other brands. Hard drive manufacturers can also reverse engineer the products of their competitors to improve their own products with minimal R&D. When you are essentially leading an entire technological field such as Nvidia is with graphics, there is no blueprint to copy. You have to create the blueprint with your own R&D. And when you are at that level of innovation and basically competing with yourself, it is logical to have a premium price; especially in times with high global inflation, employee shortages, and shortages of your main raw material (chips). I still have not seen a single YouTuber mention price margins and where Nvidia is selling these cards in relation to their normal margin goals. Because that is generally the number 1 driver of where prices are set.

Everybody should just restrain from buying GPUs at the moment, until prices are somewhat normal again. For me, a fair price would be 500 to  maximum 800 for an 8K-capable (60fps or more) new graphics card, but NEVER a 1000 or even more. If a big chunk of all the worlds CPU Enthusiasts, Gamers or even first-time buyers work together, we can make the prices drop to a reasonable price. Just don't buy them at a time like this! It's that easy.
They will sit on the shelves of NVIDIA or AMD and collect dust. If one of those companies realizes, that they can't pay their executives and stuff anymore, the only option left for making money is to get the prices adjusted not higher, but lower, to sell off a big junk of their products for being able to pay their employees.
And if they decide to slack off by doing nothing, I'm sure that the next GPU-company will be born pretty quickly to get into this market. I wouldn't be surprised if a company like apple would hop onto the GPU-train as a tech company. And if apple does it, it's not far to see Microsoft and other tech companies jumping onto the GPU train. Samsung also would get into the GPU-Market. Most tech-companies will follow soon. In short: every company with a better TECH knowhow would probably size the chance to make some new products and to get into that market to have their own share of it.

So let's wait until prices will (eventually) drop.

So people really thought XTX was going to get 1.5x uplift over a 6950. And at $995 that's a steal, and a 4080-killer.

So when the card hits 3rd party review, and it pulls in more like 1.3x or so over a 6950. Consumers were wondering if AMD lied to them, or if AMD themselves is frustrated with the final result.

The hype tapered down to reality at a steeper angle than usual for AMD. 

Personally, I look at gpu's through the lens of monitor resolution more than most people seem to. Like some reviewers talk performance:dollar ratio, some talk about just performance. Me I'm thinking what keeps 'All the Gamez' inside 60-144 hz in 4k? And then looking at prices. And then what keeps 'All the Gamez' in 60-144 in 1440p ultrawide, and how are those priced? Then 1440p, then 1080p, etc.

Anyway, point being the difference between 1.3x uplift vs 1.5x uplift, somewhat weakens the 7900 XTX's footing in the 4k bracket. Can it 4k? sure definitely. But, you're gonna have to kill some eye candy in more titles (than I had hoped) to keep frames per second floated. And turning off eye candy for fps reduces the value proposition of your 4k display (which likely wasn't cheap, at all). I'd hoped xtx would dominate 4k-on-ultra (without ray tracing), and turning on FSR would see 4k ray tracing to 60+ fps with minimal fidelity loss. 

XTX is less securely in that 4k territory than I'd hoped, and might be best suited to 1440px3440. Which is cool, but there are other $1000 options in that bracket. Really it's kinda in-between the 4k and 1440p ultrawide brackets. Which is just less marketable. 4080's performance is NOT 20-30% more (as the price would suggest), but it may be a little more securely positioned for 4k use. Is that worth an extra $200-300? I really dunno.

I think the infinity cache (or the 6nm MCD's), are holding rdna3 back. that 5nm core clocks to 3.2 Ghz like a boss. But performance only scales to 2.7 Ghz, and then jumps off a cliff (chiplet de-sync? maybe?). Right there is the difference between the slides, and the real world results. And the difference between being the cheapest rock-solid 4k card, or the cheapest semi-4k / solid-1440ultrawide card. Which isn't helpful when Fall 2022 is kinda the "GOOD 4k, finally" extravaganza.

text: To be fair, Jensen Huang didn't "forget" about the pricing fiasco he stood to correct with the 30 series. Why? Because the second customers flocked to stores & scalpers to buy overpriced GPUs during a pandemic because they just NEEDED to get their hands on the latest & greatest at the time, despite the pandemic & shortages driving prices up artificially, it told Nvidia, AMD and all the partners that people were willing to pay exorbitant amounts for new graphics cards. Hence why we have such terrible pricing structure this go around. I mean, I am not trying to put this all on the customers because obviously the pricing was set by the companies, but where exactly does pricing come from? Data. And what did the data from the 30 series show them? Customers were buying GPUs with ridiculously inflated prices. That then changes the mindset of a company. So perhaps, while we are scolding Nvidia for ripping people off and AMD for upselling an over hyped XT card, let's also scold the idiots that went out and paid twice the MSRP for a 30 series GPU that guaranteed that pricing with the 40 series would be screwed up from the beginning. As for everything else you are saying, you are spot on. Neither Nvidia, nor AMD deserve our business this generation. But again, despite the shady s*** these companies have pulled on us, especially Nvidia with their card mixups & pricing, customers flocked to buy the 4090 like it was candy, 4080s are starting to sell through and I can almost guarantee that despite these terrible reviews of the 4070ti, consumers will still be out getting them. Maybe not at a frantic pace, but it will happen. So... the cycle will continue. Companies blatantly rip off customers. Dumb customers blatantly ignore it and allow themselves to be ripped off. text:
I get that it is fashionable to hate everything about this launch, but how does it make sense to discard DLSS 3 completely? My crude understanding is that it represents a significant uplift in performance and if the game supports it there is no reason not to enable it (especially in combination with Ray Tracing). So ignoring DLSS is like running a GPU comparison suite with all settings as low as possible. Why would you not test high end hardware with all the latest game/resolution/upscaling tech enabled? 

Any argument about "unfair comparisons" just highlights the importance of properly reporting on DLSS/FSR in the first place. If the end result is that certain games perform much better for NVIDIA and others perform much better for AMD then so be it. But don't make that information opaque because you want to provide a more apples to apples comparison that has little real world value.

text: That's an easy one to explain.    For a GPU, you get greater memory bandwidth from more VRAM chips.    So, if there are 8 chips, you get a certain amount of bandwidth, 32 bit per chip would give you 256 bit memory bandwidth.   Go to 12GB of VRAM, so you now have 12 chips for 384 bit memory bandwidth.   Obviously then, this doesn't work for the 3060 which didn't have a 384 bit bus, so, what if these are 2GB per chip instead of 1GB per chip.   So, 8GB version then ends up being 128 bit memory bandwidth and the 12GB version has 192 bit memory bandwidth.   Those numbers sound correct based on what I remember.   More VRAM CHIPS=faster due to memory bandwidth.

author: @MatoVuc

text:
When Nvidia showed off a chart comparing 30-series and 40-series performance and the chosen games were F1 22, Darktide, Miles Morales, Cyberpunk 2077 w/ RT Overdrive, A Plague Tale: Requiem, Portal with RTX and MS Flight Simulator, my first thought was "Hey, don't all those games support DLSS 3?" Moments later, they explicitly said it was delivering an average of 1.8x performance across a range of titles "with the power of DLSS 3" so it was pretty obvious what they were talking about if you actually watched the video.

It's almost impressive how you manage to dance around testing the actual claims they made. They mentioned (verbally) maxing framerates on 1440p monitors, and yet for a lot of titles you didn't even do 1440p testing. In the titles you did 1440p testing for, it was more comparable to the 3090 Ti than at 4k, yet in the oh-so-important Cyberpunk 2077 performance claim, you only saw fit to do 4k testing? They also verbally mentioned DLSS 3, but you explicitly refused to use it in that same benchmark. They also mentioned the RT Overdrive mode for Cyberpunk, but presumably not having access to that, you didn't test it, which is at least understandable. I will wonder aloud, if the 4070 Ti is barely faster than the 3090 Ti at 4k in Cyberpunk 2077, and presumably has a wider performance gap at 1440p, and further gap with RT Overdrive, is it unthinkable that with frame generation they could get 3x the framerate as the 3090 Ti? I get it, you can't test RT Overdrive right now, but it doesn't seem like you even tried to test the other parts of the claim. You did the least favorable test you could in the spirit of "Cyberpunk with RT" which isn't so much testing Nvidia's ability to tell the truth, as your ability to test their actual claims.

I usually enjoy your flavor of sarcasm/skepticism but the level of benchmarking you did here and the conclusions you drew from them feel like a disservice to your viewers.

text:
@joshbrobud8358  Yeah basically. Let's not pretend like Nvidia could sell a 4070 TI FE for $300 and still make a profit. When games continually push higher resolutions and fidelity, there is only so much you can do from an engineering perspective to deliver more horsepower for the same cost, and when customers are asking for that same hat trick every two years for forever (which even without considering investor pressure is completely unrealistic) while you are required by law to appease investor demands to increase profit margins it is a small wonder that nvidia has kept largely reasonable prices that beat their previous generations frame/dollar value on most generations. Even an inflation adjusted price of $440 for the 970 at release is still something that will never be seen on a 70 class again for msrp. Now are these cards overpriced and badly named? Of course they are. But the second Nvidia changed the Titan series to the xx90 series so it could be included in there "gaming" marketing we could honestly all see this coming. And anyone who thinks $300 is reasonable for a 4070 TI doesn't know how both inflation and general transistor costs work. Thats another thing, the price of transistors have stopped going down a few years back, it's why the PS4 and Xbone never got a price cut to their slim or 8.5 gen models and the ps5 and xboxsx aren't expected to go down in price ever. A decent chunk of that value gain from gen to gen was from the fact that they could get more transistors for close to the same cost, now all they can do is make the design smarter and more efficient which only takes you so far when the general price of everything is going up. I think Nvidia is to some extent gouging but if they weren't then the price of the 4070 TI wasn't gonna go below $700 anyways with the current chip design. The R&D and the profit marigins promised to investors were largely locked in years ago in the height of GPU demand and the crypto market boom. In an alternate timeline where the pandemic never happened and the crypto bubble never reinflated Nvidia may have put more money into R&D and that R&D resulting more productive without lockdown conditions and released a $600 card with 4070 TI horsepower or perhaps even a bit more. I think the 5000 series Nvidia is gonna have a major redesign of their chip which will bring it back in line with value propositions like how the 30 series did when the 20 failed to impress and was considered overpriced. But a 5070 will never be $300.

And let's be honest here, the consoles have horsepower considered equivalent to a RTX 2070 with less efficient RT. An 8 gig 3060 TI will last you until the PS6 and Xbox Series Zeta Pro launch and those are hovering right around that $440 inflation adjusted 970 price mark. If you are willing to go used just know that I managed to score a 3070 TI for only $450, pair it with a 5600x or 5800x3d on sale or whatever 13th gen intel core is the best atm and you are good to go until 2028. Unless you are trying to max out Cyberpunk or Flight Simulator on your 4k high refresh rate display the 4000 series is overkill and the biggest of them all can't even be utilized fully anyways till better cpus come out.

text: It is kinda sad that none of the Tech. channels talk about the cache change on the GPU. Most people think that the performance gain comes from a "new generation" of "cores" on the GPU. which is rather false. Boiling it down, they are just switches flipping between 1 and 0. What is new, is frame generation  and the almost 3 times increase of the on die cache. Just look at the number of transistors on these new dies, almost triple of the last generation but they only have at best 50% more cores. What are all the other transistors? Cache. More cache better performance. Just look at AMDs 3D Cache CPUs. There is no generational change between RTX 3000 and 4000 series cores. That is why the 4000 series is still bad at RT. They just dumped more cache on the die and added frame generation to DLSS 3.

text:
So let me get this straight, about 70% of this benchmark is about rasterisation performance only. Maybe 1 minute is spent on ray tracing performance. And then 2 minutes spent on power draw. Then when testing the RT performance, DLSS3 is purposely disabled to "level the playing field", rather than showing the improvement over previous versions of DLSS and thus giving a more realistic picture of the actual performance with DLSS enabled.

What I take away from this review, is that in RT titles the 4070Ti performs on par with the 3080 or 3090 and almost consistently beats or equals the 7900XTX.
It does this while retailing for under 1k euro, including taxes, and while using significantly less power to do so.
Even in rasterisation titles, the performance isn't bad given the FPS-per-watt differences over the 30xx or 7900 series.

Meanwhile a 3080 and 3090 still retail for 1k and 1300 euro respectively, 1400 buys you a 4080... And as a complete joke, the 7900XTX retails at near as makes no difference 1200 euro.

While hating on "not enough generational uplift" for the 4070Ti, the very same graphs show that this kind of performance uplift is in line with the 3060 performing at par with a 2070 or a 3070 performing similar to a 2080. So while underwhelming, it's basically par for the course for RTX cards.

Yes nVidia still has egg on it's face because of the unlaunching of the 4080 12GB and now relaunching it as the 4070Ti. Still in the end to me, it's probably the most worthwhile GPU out there at the moment.
The performance is solid, it's cheaper than the 3080 and 3090 that it effectively replaces. It's more power efficient, which given current electricity prices is very much relevant.

I dunno Steve, but if this sets the tone for your reviews for this generation. I'm sorry but you're losing your edge here. As you seem to basically ignore half of the GPU you're reviewing. Where's the GPGPU testing? What about Tensor performance? I'd hate to accuse you of bias, but this is a half arsed job at best. So I guess your first review of 2023 makes a good candidate for the next t-shirt of disappointment.

text:
@pandemicneetbux2110  The gtx 1000 series were the single most overpriced GPU generation of GPUs at MSRP(FE MSRP).
Nvidia sold them at 90-138% profit margin.

The gtx 1080 is the single most overpriced GPU ever. 312mm^2 die size, sub-mid range GPU sold with 5.5$ per 1GB DDR5 VRAM for 700$ MSRP(FE MSRP became MSRP shortly after launch even for 3rd party cards)... 

The RTX 2080 was 545mm^2 with 19$ per 1GB of GDDR6 VRAM for 700$ is a much more normal price, still very high, as Nvidia sold the rtx 2000 series at 50-60% profit margins, but nowhere near the 90-138% of the gtx 1000 series. That's why their stocks took a dive in 2018.

Also RDNA1 and RDNA2 would have been great if AMD didn't double their profit margins from 23% to 45% in 2019 with the release of RDNA1 and Zen2 and then further increase them to almost 60% in 2020 with the release of RDNA2 and Zen3...

I'd say RDNA3 is not disappointing, the price is. AMD can't compete with Nvidia in terms of power efficiency anymore, because they are using chiplets. Chiplets(Multi-Chip Modules) consume a lot more power than monolithic dies.

Plus AMD's RDNA3 GPUs are on 5nm, while Nvidia's are on 4nm(5nm+). 4nm runs 11% faster(high clock speeds) at 22% less power draw and is 7% smaller than 5nm per transistor. So combine that with AMD using chiplets and AMD will consume more power.

The matter of the fact is that BOTH AMD and Nvidia suck. Any GPU that is above 225W and requires more than 1x 8 pin cable is absolutetly stupid... AMD and Nvidia are trying to make super cars be the standard... makes no sense.

Even according to both AMD and Nvidia during their launches in 2016, 2017, 2018 and 2019, 80% of people buy GPUs under 200$ and 95%+ bought GPUs under 400$, now that was up to 2019, add in about 20-25% on top of that due to inflation and let's say 80% buy under 250$ and 95%+ buy under 500$...

And this is proven by steam's survey, which isn't entirely accurate, but a good representation. The top 3 GPUs are the gtx 1650, GTX 1060, GTX 1050Ti, number 4 is rtx 2060.

text:
​ @johngray3449  true, the 4080 is on the lower end compared to other cards. 

The og Titan however also had 75% more Cuda cores than the GTX 680. 
The reason for this was quite simple: Due to AMD not competing with the Titan, they could sell their cheap Midrange Chip as competitor to AMDs high end chip. 

When AMD became competitive again, Nvidia had to put the big chip on to the 780. 

With Maxwell AMD could never really compete with the 980 ti, so the big chip never made it into the 80 class. 

Then came Pascal, which was a massive improvement over Maxwell. This time AMD could not even compete with the GTX 1080 (Midrange Chip). This is why it initially cost 700 USD. 

Turing was a generation where AMD had absolutely nothing that could compete, so the first price hikes happend. 

RDNA2 was pretty good from the get go, so they had to put the GA102 on the 3080. 

This Gen looks like Pascal or Turing again. 
I really hope Intel does something here, because AMD is essentially the reason we now have a monopoly in the dGPU sector.

text:
It's really easy to understand why this card is a Ti - historically, Nvidia has used the Ti brand to slip in an intermediate model between 2 existing cards in the product stack (or above for the 90 card), usually after the fact. That's often been a small cut down of the card above it, a year in, to attract more buyers, but the closest thing to a rule here is just that it sits between existing cards.

Nvidia had designed a 4080 and a 4070 already, but then they made another card in between and tried to pretend it was also a 4080. Because they've already got  a 4070 in the pipeline, when public backlash forced them to rebrand the slower 4080 the only name they had unoccupied was the 70Ti, as that product hasn't been developed yet. It winds up seeming superfluous because what's previously happened is that the Ti is supposed to be an upgrade to the existing lower end card, but they tried to trick people into buying less GPU for more money with a fake 4080 and as an alternative to throwing the cards in the bin this is what they had left.
